questions.prompt: Why do applications use a database connection pool?
options: Opening a connection is expensive, so connections are reused across requests
To limit the number of tables
questions.explanation: Creating connections costs network round trips, authentication and server resources. A pool keeps a set ready for reuse.

questions.prompt: What happens when every connection in the pool is in use and another request needs one?
options: It waits up to a configured timeout, then fails if none becomes free
A new connection is always created without limit
The query runs without a connection
questions.explanation: Pools have a maximum size. Excess requests queue; if the wait exceeds the timeout (e.g. HikariCP's connectionTimeout), they fail.

questions.prompt: Making a connection pool much larger always improves performance.
questions.explanation: Beyond the point the database can run efficiently, more connections cause contention, memory use and context switching. Larger pools can make things slower.

questions.prompt: An instance handles 200 req/s. Each request holds a DB connection for 30 ms on average. What is the average number of busy connections, and is a pool of 10 enough?
questions.code:
rate = 200      # req/s
hold = 0.030    # s per request
options: 6 on average; 10 gives some headroom for bursts but should be verified under load
questions.explanation: Little's Law: 200 x 0.03 = 6 busy on average. Peaks will be higher, so 10 is plausible but must be checked with pool-wait metrics.

questions.prompt: Which pool metrics should you graph during a load test? Select all that apply.
options: Number of tables in the database
questions.explanation: Active, pending and acquire time show utilization and saturation of the pool. Table count is not a pool metric.

questions.prompt: Each request makes an HTTP call to a slow partner API while holding a DB connection from a transaction it opened earlier. What is the risk?
options: Connections are held during the remote call, so the pool exhausts when the partner is slow; release DB resources before the external call
The partner API will see the DB connection
questions.explanation: Hold time includes everything done while the connection is checked out. Slow external calls inflate it and starve other requests.

questions.prompt: 10 app instances each have a pool max of 50. The database allows 300 connections. During autoscaling to 10 instances, errors appear: "too many connections". What is the fix?
options: Size pools so instances x pool max stays below the DB limit (with room for admin/maintenance), or put a connection proxy in front of the DB
questions.explanation: 500 possible connections exceed the 300 limit. Pool sizing must account for the total across all instances.

questions.prompt: A web server has 200 worker threads. Under load, CPU is 20%, thread pool active = 200, queued requests grow, and thread dumps show most threads waiting on HTTP calls to a slow service. What do you recommend?
options: Set sensible timeouts and a bulkhead (separate limited pool) for the slow dependency, or use async I/O, so it cannot consume every worker thread
questions.explanation: Threads are blocked waiting, not computing. Isolating the slow dependency and bounding its waiting time protects the rest of the service.

coding.title: Simulate a bounded pool
coding.prompt:
Simulate a connection pool. Write `simulate(requests, size, timeout)` where each request is `(arrival_ms, hold_ms)` sorted by arrival. A request takes a free connection immediately if one exists; otherwise it waits for the earliest connection to free up. If its wait would exceed `timeout` ms, it fails (and never takes a connection). Return `(succeeded, failed, max_wait)` where `max_wait` is the longest wait among successful requests.

Example: `simulate([(0, 100), (0, 100), (10, 50)], 2, 200)` returns `(3, 0, 90)`.
coding.solution:
import heapq

def simulate(requests, size, timeout):
    free_at = [0] * size
    heapq.heapify(free_at)
    ok = failed = max_wait = 0
    for arrival, hold in requests:
        earliest = free_at[0]
        start = max(arrival, earliest)
        wait = start - arrival
        if wait > timeout:
            failed += 1
            continue
        heapq.heapreplace(free_at, start + hold)
        ok += 1
        max_wait = max(max_wait, wait)
    return ok, failed, max_wait
coding.explanation: A min-heap of 'time each connection becomes free' always gives the earliest available connection. This mirrors how pool timeouts turn slow queries (long holds) into errors for unrelated requests.
hints: Track when each connection becomes free, starting at 0.
`heapq` gives you the earliest free time at index 0.
Only replace a heap entry when the request succeeds.
